expected_evidence: geological: a distinct Younger Dryas boundary (YDB) layer across North American sediment sequences showing elevated iridium/platinum group elements, magnetic spherules, and a 'black mat' organic-rich layer marking abrupt ecological transition (~12,900 cal BP)
geological/astronomical: shock-metamorphosed quartz grains, meltglass, and nanodiamonds (hexagonal lonsdaleite) in the YDB layer consistent with impact or airburst thermal/pressure signatures
astronomical: an identifiable impact crater or strewnfield of the appropriate age in North America or under the Laurentide ice sheet (none confirmed to date)
material/archaeological: abrupt disappearance of Clovis-culture diagnostic artifacts and a hiatus/disruption in the Clovis archaeological record coinciding with the boundary layer
genetic: ancient-DNA-based extinction/population-decline chronologies for megafauna (mammoth, mastodon, horse, etc.) showing a sharp synchronous decline or bottleneck at ~10,950 uncal BP
geological: continent-wide correlation of biomass-burning markers (soot, charcoal peaks) and abrupt climate proxies (temperature, dust) coincident with the proposed impact horizon

model_prior: prior published hypotheses/debate in the geoarchaeological literature explicitly proposing a cosmic impact trigger for Younger Dryas onset and megafaunal extinction (the 'Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis')
response.rationale: This hypothesis corresponds to the well-known (and contested) Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis (YDIH), dated to ~10,950 radiocarbon/cal BP, so I treated the period as 'younger-dryas' for scoring purposes despite the nominal 'unspecified' label. Using that row: geological detectability is relatively high (0.65) and astronomical detectability is the highest of all evidence kinds (0.7) for this period, because impact/airburst signatures (iridium/PGE anomalies, spherules, nanodiamonds, shocked quartz) and any surviving crater would be searched for using well-established, mature geological and remote-sensing methods, and 12,900-year-old sedimentary layers are well within the preservation window of Quaternary geology. Material (0.35) and genetic (0.3) evidence are moderately detectable — Clovis-era archaeological sites and megafaunal remains are reasonably well sampled in North America, though taphonomic loss, incomplete site survey, and dating-resolution limits reduce confidence in synchroneity claims. Model-prior detectability (0.3) reflects that this is a known, actively debated academic hypothesis (model-prior, unverified beyond training recall) rather than a settled fact — the YDB impact markers reported by some researchers (e.g., platinum/iridium spikes, nanodiamonds) have been independently disputed or failed to replicate at many sites, and no confirmed impact crater of the right age/size has been identified in North America or beneath the Laurentide ice sheet. Given the high astronomical/geological detectability scores, the absence of an unambiguous crater and the contested/non-replicated status of chemical markers is more evidentially informative here than in low-detectability periods — but a small airburst (Tunguska-style) could plausibly leave no crater at all, which weakens that absence as decisive counter-evidence. Overall, evidence of this type could plausibly have survived and been found given the timeframe and detectability profile, but the mixed and disputed empirical record to date does not strongly confirm the hypothesis; I set the adjustment at 0.45, an average weighted toward the higher-detectability geological/astronomical channels balanced against weaker material/genetic/model-prior support.
